summary: Specifies WebDAV SEARCH, a set of methods, headers, and properties that add searching to HTTP-based WebDAV. A client sends search criteria and the server returns matching resources, so the client does not have to fetch and scan everything itself. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A big shared folder on a website is hard to look through by hand. This lets you ask the server to search it for you and give back just the matching files.

questions: what does the search method do in webdav
subtitle: A way to ask a WebDAV server to search its resources and send back only the matches.

tldr.problem: A WebDAV client that wants to find resources by their properties or content would otherwise have to fetch and scan everything itself.
tldr.mechanism: The SEARCH method sends an XML query to a search arbiter, which runs it on the server and returns the matches in the standard WebDAV 207 multistatus format. One query grammar, DAV:basicsearch, is mandatory.
tldr.outcome: Clients can use server-side search without learning a new protocol. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 5323 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its Appendix B names open ideas such as result paging and collation support as candidates for future work.

sections.title: What WebDAV SEARCH Is
sections.content:
RFC 5323 defines WebDAV SEARCH, an application of HTTP/1.1 that forms a lightweight search protocol. It transports queries and result sets so that clients can use server-side search facilities. It grew out of earlier work by the IETF DASL working group, and the RFC uses the names "WebDAV SEARCH" and "DASL" interchangeably.

DASL relies on the resource and property model of RFC 4918 and does not change it. It only lets clients reach DAV-modeled resources through a search run by the server. It consists of the SEARCH method, feature discovery through the DASL response header, optional grammar schema discovery, and one mandatory grammar, DAV:basicsearch.

The RFC also explains why it defines elements in the DAV: XML namespace even though that is normally reserved for IETF working group work: the specification had already seen significant deployment when the working group closed down.
sections.eli5: It is a way to ask a website's file collection a question, like "which pictures are bigger than this?", and get just the answer instead of checking every file yourself.

sections.title: The SEARCH Method
sections.content:
The client sends a SEARCH request to a search arbiter, which is any resource that supports the method. The Request-URI names the arbiter. It is not a new kind of resource and does not even have to be WebDAV-compliant. The method only carries the query and the result set. The query grammar decides what the query means, and the grammar also decides how the arbiter relates to the search scope.

The request body is a DAV:searchrequest or a DAV:query-schema-discovery element, in text/xml or application/xml. Its single child names the query grammar. The server must process such a body. SEARCH is a safe method: it only runs a query and returns a result.

Four preconditions can fail a request: the grammar is unsupported, schema discovery is unsupported, multiple scopes were given but are not supported, or the scope is invalid. An invalid scope gets an error body naming DAV:search-scope-valid; the RFC's example is a 409 Conflict where one scope resource returned 404.
sections.eli5: You write your question on a card and hand it to the librarian. The card says which question style you are using, and the librarian tells you if they do not know that style.

sections.title: The 207 Multistatus Response
sections.content:
A successful search returns 207 (Multistatus) in the WebDAV multistatus format. There is one DAV:response for each matching resource, holding its DAV:href and a DAV:propstat. The RFC relaxes the usual rule of at least one response so that an empty result can be expressed. Results SHOULD NOT be cached. If several URIs map to one resource, a server SHOULD report only one, and clients can use DAV:resource-id to spot duplicates.

A server MAY cap the number of results, for example to save effort. When it does, it still answers 207, SHOULD include the partial results, and adds a response for the search arbiter URI with status 507 (Insufficient Storage). Any partial results MUST follow the order the client asked for.

Other failures use an appropriate status code and SHOULD carry a condition body as defined in RFC 3253.
sections.eli5: The librarian brings back a list with one line per matching folder. If there were too many, the librarian hands over some and adds a note saying "I stopped early."

sections.title: Discovering Grammars and Schemas
sections.content:
Servers MUST let clients discover which query grammars an arbiter supports. A client sends OPTIONS. If the resource supports SEARCH, the server lists SEARCH in the Allow header and includes a DASL header whose value is a list of grammar URIs, for example DASL: <DAV:basicsearch>. Servers that support RFC 3253 or RFC 3744 must also report SEARCH in DAV:supported-method-set and support the DAV:supported-query-grammar-set property.

Knowing the grammar is not enough to write a query, because the grammar does not say which properties may be used. Servers MAY therefore offer Query Schema Discovery. The client sends a SEARCH whose root element is DAV:query-schema-discovery, and the multistatus response carries a DAV:query-schema inside each response. The schema can depend on both the arbiter and the scope: two collections on one server may expose different properties.
sections.eli5: Before asking, you can check which question styles the librarian understands, and even ask which things in the cabinet you are allowed to ask about.

sections.title: The DAV:basicsearch Grammar
sections.content:
Every DASL server MUST accept DAV:basicsearch and MAY accept others. A query has up to five parts:

  • DAV:select chooses the properties returned, either DAV:allprop or a DAV:prop list.
  • DAV:from sets the scope: one or more DAV:scope elements, each with a DAV:href and a DAV:depth of 0, 1 or infinity. Multiple scopes are optional.
  • DAV:where holds the search condition.
  • DAV:orderby sorts the results; earlier comparisons matter more, and ascending is the default.
  • DAV:limit asks the server to return at most DAV:nresults responses, which the server MAY disregard.

A relative scope is taken relative to the Request-URI. With DAV:include-versions the scope also covers all versions of version-controlled resources. If a limited result is also ordered, the results returned SHOULD be those that order highest.
sections.eli5: A question has parts: what details you want back, which shelves to look on, the rule a folder must match, how to sort the answers, and the most answers you want.

sections.title: Operators and Matching Rules
sections.content:
The where condition is built from operators that evaluate to TRUE, FALSE or UNKNOWN. A resource is included only if the condition is TRUE. Comparison operators are DAV:eq, DAV:lt, DAV:lte, DAV:gt and DAV:gte; logic operators are DAV:and, DAV:or and DAV:not. Others include DAV:is-collection and DAV:is-defined. A query using an operator the server does not support gets 422 (Unprocessable Entity).

A property that would fail a PROPFIND is treated as NULL, and NULL sorts below every other value, while an empty string is not NULL. Literals are compared as strings by default, except that content length is an unsigned integer and dates use the ISO-8601 subset of RFC 4918. DAV:typed-literal forces a typed comparison using xsi:type, and a comparison that cannot be cast is UNKNOWN. The caseless attribute, optional, requests caseless matching.

Optional operators include DAV:like, with _ for exactly one character and % for zero or more; DAV:contains, a content search whose exact behavior is left to the server; and the language operators DAV:language-defined and DAV:language-matches. For DAV:contains servers SHOULD return a DAV:score from zero to 10000, where higher means more relevant. Appendix A defines the three-valued logic, for example UNKNOWN and FALSE is FALSE, and UNKNOWN or TRUE is TRUE.
sections.eli5: You can say things like "bigger than", "named like" or "mentions this word". If a folder is missing the detail you asked about, the answer is "don't know", and those folders are left out.

sections.title: Security and Scalability
sections.content:
All the security considerations of HTTP/1.1 and RFC 4918 apply. The key rule is that a query MUST NOT let clients retrieve anything they could not get through GET or PROPFIND. Constraints on properties the client cannot read are evaluated as if the property did not exist, and content constraints without read access are evaluated as if a GET would return a 4xx status.

Servers should prepare for denial-of-service attacks, such as a query whose result set is expensive to compute or send. The RFC also warns that XML external entities are untrustworthy and can cause scalability problems. Grammar URIs identify grammars, and applications SHOULD NOT try to retrieve them even if they start with http://.

For IANA, the document registers the DASL header field name for HTTP with status standard. Appendix B lists ideas left for later, such as collation support, result counts and result paging.
sections.eli5: The librarian must never show you a folder you are not allowed to open, even by answering your question cleverly. And one huge question could wear the librarian out, so servers need to be ready for that.
